questions.question: A payslip shows a gross salary of R9 500,00, with deductions of PAYE R760,00, UIF R95,00 and pension R475,00. Calculate the net income, add the household's other income of R900,00 rent and R1 130,00 from sewing, and explain why the gross figure may not be used in a budget.
questions.expected_answer: Total deductions: R760 + R95 + R475 = R1 330,00. Net income: R9 500 − R1 330 = R8 170,00. Total household income: R8 170 + R900 + R1 130 = R10 200,00 per month. The gross figure may not be used because that money never reaches the household — the employer pays the deductions over on the employee's behalf, so only the net amount can actually be spent. A second error follows from the first: because the deductions never arrive as income, they must not be listed again as expenses, or the same money is subtracted twice. It is also worth noting that the R1 130 from sewing varies from month to month, so a careful budget either uses the lowest recent figure or plans for its absence.

questions.question: Distinguish fixed, variable and occasional expenses, giving examples from the household budget, and explain the test used to classify an item such as electricity.
questions.expected_answer: Fixed expenses are the same amount each month regardless of behaviour: rent R3 000, funeral policy R180, school fees R450 and the phone contract R199, totalling R3 829,00. Variable expenses change with how much is used or bought: groceries R2 600, prepaid electricity R750, taxi fare R880, airtime and data R240, and toiletries and cleaning R320, totalling R4 790,00. Occasional expenses arrive only a few times a year but are provided for monthly — R400 for uniforms and stationery and R500 for December and family events, totalling R900,00 — and setting money aside in advance like this is called provisioning. The classification test is not "does it come every month?" but "does the amount change with how much I use?" Electricity arrives monthly yet the amount responds to use, so it is variable; rent arrives monthly and does not respond to behaviour, so it is fixed. This matters because when money is short, only the variable items can be cut within the month.

questions.question: A vetkoek stall has fixed costs of R600,00 a month, a variable cost of R3,50 per vetkoek and a selling price of R8,00. Calculate the break-even point, explain how you round it and why, and work out the profit in a month when 312 vetkoek are sold.
questions.expected_answer: Each vetkoek contributes R8,00 − R3,50 = R4,50 towards the fixed costs, so the break-even number is R600 ÷ R4,50 = 133,33. This must be rounded UP to 134. Rounding down to 133 gives income of 133 × R8,00 = R1 064,00 against a total cost of R600 + (133 × R3,50) = R600 + R465,50 = R1 065,50 — a loss of R1,50 — while 134 gives income of R1 072,00 against a total cost of R600 + R469,00 = R1 069,00, a profit of R3,00. For 312 vetkoek: income = 312 × R8,00 = R2 496,00; total cost = R600 + (312 × R3,50) = R600 + R1 092,00 = R1 692,00; profit = R2 496 − R1 692 = R804,00. The answer should be written as a sentence: the stall breaks even at 134 vetkoek a month and, selling about 312, makes a profit of R804,00.
